prose.summary: A sales representative gets a defined patch, a quota, and a CRM that tracks whether you hit it. What separates it from account executive work is the stage of the relationship: reps spend more time finding and qualifying accounts, AEs spend more time closing and expanding ones already in the door, and postings for this role lean B2B rather than consumer.
prose.day_to_day: Mornings tend to start in the CRM, checking which leads moved overnight and which calls are due. A rep might spend two or three hours on outbound calls and emails, then break for a client visit or a video demo in the afternoon. Fridays often mean pipeline review with a manager, going through the forecast line by line and explaining why a deal slipped a stage. There's a particular satisfaction in watching a cold account you opened six months ago sign, especially when nobody else on the team thought it would close. Roughly half the week is solo prep and admin (updating records, building quotes in Excel), the other half is calls, meetings, and the odd trade show or site visit. Expense reports and CRM hygiene eat more time than anyone expects going in.
prose.work_environment: Most of this work happens from an office or a home desk, with travel layered in for client visits, industry events, or regional territory coverage. The 26 percent remote share reflects that a meaningful chunk of the job (calls, CRM updates, proposal writing) can happen anywhere, but face time with clients and quarterly team meetings still pull people back into a room. Bad weeks cluster around quarter-end, when everyone is trying to close what's stalled, and around trade show season if the employer sells anything physical. Hours are usually standard business hours, though calls with clients in a different time zone or an evening dinner with a prospect are not unusual.
prose.getting_in: Most postings want a degree (162 of the measured listings require one, 21 prefer it, only 9 waive it), but the field is friendlier to relevant experience than the raw count suggests: two years is the median asked for, and a strong record in retail, hospitality, or a junior sales-support role often substitutes for pedigree in interviews. The degree itself rarely needs to be in business; employers care more about whether you can talk to a stranger and follow up on time. The stall point is usually the first job: getting hired with zero sales experience is harder than moving from a first sales role to a second. Language matters more here than in most Business roles measured, given the concentration of openings in Switzerland and Germany, so German fluency alongside English is a real gate in a large share of these postings. Budget three to six months for a first sales role search if you're starting from an adjacent customer-facing job, longer if you're starting cold.
prose.ladder: Early on you own a list of accounts and a number. Move up and you start owning a territory or vertical, then a team's number instead of just your own, which is where the fork happens: some reps move into sales management and start living in one-on-ones and coaching, others deliberately stay individual contributors and chase bigger accounts or better commission structures instead of headcount. The jump usually happens two to four years in, once you've carried a full quota through at least one down cycle and shown you can forecast honestly rather than optimistically. Account executive is a common lateral step (the highest-match route out at 88 percent match coming in the other direction) and often pays better without requiring management.
prose.suits: People who like a scoreboard tend to do well here: the job gives you a number every week and tells you plainly whether you beat it, and there's a real charge in watching a quarter come together in the last ten days. It rewards people who don't take a no personally and who genuinely enjoy the puzzle of figuring out what a stranger needs versus what they say they need. People who leave usually wanted more predictability in their income or their calendar than commission-based work provides, or they wanted to build something technical rather than sell it. If constant rejection wears on you faster than it energizes you, the variable pay structure will grind rather than motivate.
prose.misconceptions: Outsiders assume the job is mostly talking, when in practice a large share of the week is written: emails, CRM notes, proposals, follow-up sequences. Another common assumption is that a naturally outgoing personality is the main qualifier; what separates good reps from mediocre ones is discipline around follow-up and honest forecasting, not charisma in the room.
prose.who_qualifies: Account executives transfer in almost completely (88 percent match), since the core skills (pipeline management, CRM discipline, negotiation) are the same, just applied earlier in the sales cycle. Real estate developers (60 percent) and customer success managers (51 percent) also carry over well: developers bring deal structuring and client relationship skills, CSMs bring the account-management and renewal conversations that map onto expansion selling. Customer support specialists (38 percent) bring product knowledge and patience but usually need to build outbound and negotiation muscle from scratch. Real estate agents transfer in at only 28 percent, since licensed selling has its own compliance and process layer that doesn't map cleanly onto B2B sales.
prose.what_the_numbers_miss: None of this captures what a bad territory feels like: a patch with no existing accounts and a quota set by someone who's never worked it. It also can't show you the difference between a manager who protects your pipeline from reorgs and one who doesn't, which matters more to year-to-year satisfaction than almost anything else measured here.

steps.how: Retail, hospitality, or a support desk role for six to twelve months teaches you to read people and handle rejection, and it gives you a concrete story for interviews. Employers hiring for this role care less about the label on your first job than whether you can point to a time you talked someone into something.

steps.do: Learn a CRM before you need one
steps.how: Salesforce shows up in 13 percent of postings and general CRM skill in 25 percent, making it the single most common technical ask. Free trial accounts and Salesforce's own Trailhead modules take a weekend to get comfortable with, and being able to say you've built a pipeline view in an interview separates you from candidates who've only used a spreadsheet.

steps.do: Apply to entry-level B2B sales roles
steps.how: Target postings that state two years or fewer of experience required (the median asked for across this role) and mention training or ramp programs, since those are built for people without a sales title yet. Expect the search itself to take one to three months depending on your market and language fit, longer in Switzerland or Germany if you don't already speak German.

The first ninety days on the job are usually ramp: shadowing calls, learning the product, building your own pipeline from nothing. You'll know you've made it past the hardest part when you close your first deal you sourced yourself, not one handed to you by marketing.

steps.do: Build a track record across a full year
steps.how: Twelve months gives you a number to point to (quota attainment, deals closed, average deal size) and shows you can handle a slow quarter without falling apart. This is the record that gets you promoted internally or recruited for an account executive role, which is the most common and highest-paying next step.

prose.tools: CRM software is the real gatekeeper: some version of it shows up in a quarter of postings, and Salesforce specifically in 13 percent, so fluency there gets you past the first screen. Sales and business-development skill (24 and 15 percent) are less about a specific tool and more about how you run a call and a follow-up sequence. Excel still matters for anyone building quotes or tracking territory data by hand, and SAP appears often enough (9 percent) to matter if you're selling into larger industrial or manufacturing accounts. SaaS-specific selling (12 percent) is its own dialect, with shorter sales cycles and more emphasis on trial conversion than traditional B2B.

industries.name: SaaS and software
industries.note: Shorter sales cycles, more inbound leads, and heavy reliance on demo calls and trial conversions rather than long relationship-building.

industries.name: Manufacturing and industrial
industries.note: Longer cycles, more in-person visits, and SAP or ERP familiarity matters more than in software sales.

industries.name: Consumer goods and brewing
industries.note: Relationship-driven, often territory-based, with a physical product and distributor relationships to manage alongside the sale itself.

industries.name: Professional services
industries.note: Selling intangible expertise, longer trust-building cycles, and often a smaller number of larger accounts per rep.

specializations.name: SaaS sales
specializations.why: Twelve percent of postings already specify SaaS experience, and the shorter cycles and recurring revenue model reward reps who master trial-to-paid conversion rather than one-time deal closing.

specializations.name: Enterprise B2B accounts
specializations.why: Larger deals mean longer cycles and more stakeholders, but also materially higher commission ceilings; SAP or ERP familiarity (9 percent of postings) is a common entry point into this track.

specializations.name: Vertical specialist (brewing, industrial goods)
specializations.why: Brewing shows up in 10 percent of postings, a reminder that deep product knowledge in a specific physical-goods vertical can make you the only rep a client will take a call from, insulating you from generic sales competition.

pros: Closing a deal you sourced and nurtured yourself from a cold list gives a specific kind of satisfaction that inherited accounts never quite match.
Commission structures mean a good quarter shows up in your paycheck immediately, not two years later after a review cycle.
The skills transfer almost anywhere: account executive roles alone show an 88 percent match, so the ceiling isn't capped by this one title.
You get a clear, weekly answer to whether you're doing well, which suits people who dislike ambiguous performance reviews.
cons: Variable pay means a slow quarter hits your income directly, not just your mood.
Rejection is constant and undifferentiated: most calls and emails go nowhere, and the job requires making the next one anyway.
CRM admin and expense reporting eat real hours that don't feel like selling but are graded as part of the job.
Territory and lead quality vary wildly by employer, and a bad patch can suppress your numbers no matter how good your calls are.

faq.q: how long does it take to become a sales representative
faq.a: Most people get in within three to six months of starting to look, especially coming from another customer-facing job like retail or support. The bigger time investment is the first year on the job itself, which is usually needed to build a track record that opens up better roles.

faq.q: do you need a degree to be a sales representative
faq.a: Most postings for this role ask for one (162 require it against just 9 that waive it), but the degree rarely needs to be business-specific. Employers weigh a demonstrated ability to prospect and close over the subject on the diploma, so a relevant work history can offset a less relevant degree.

faq.q: is being a sales representative a good career right now
faq.a: It's a solid entry point into business careers generally, given how cleanly it feeds into account executive, customer success, and even real estate roles measured here. The trade-off is income variability in exchange for skills that transfer almost anywhere, which suits some people far more than others.

faq.q: can a sales representative work remotely
faq.a: Partially: about a quarter of postings measured here are remote, reflecting that calls and CRM work travel well but client visits and team pipeline reviews often don't. Fully remote roles exist mostly in SaaS, where the entire sales cycle can run over video.

faq.q: sales representative vs account executive, what's the difference
faq.a: Reps spend more time finding and qualifying new accounts, while account executives spend more time closing and growing accounts already identified or partially warmed up. The two roles share an 88 percent skill overlap, so moving between them is one of the most common and lowest-friction transitions in sales.
